system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2138-02-06 18:49:00 to 2138-02-07 16:09:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for post-procedural monitoring following a scheduled flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation and endobronchial biopsy for recurrent tracheal stenosis related to relapsing polychondritis. He tolerated the procedure well with no respiratory compromise. Post-procedural pain was managed with acetaminophen and oxycodone, and his symptoms improved over the hospital stay. He had mild bloody tracheal discharge, which was expected. Laboratory results showed elevated white blood cell count, attributed to inflammation rather than infection. Chest imaging before and after the procedure showed no complications such as pneumothorax. He was discharged home with a short supply of oxycodone, instructions to continue his chronic medications including prednisone and methotrexate, and follow-up appointments scheduled with interventional pulmonology, rheumatology, and infectious disease.
problems: Other specified diseases of upper respiratory tract

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You’re here today for your scheduled bronchoscopy and balloon dilation to help open up your airway. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay, a bit nervous. My breathing’s been worse lately, especially when I walk. Is this going to help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the procedure should help. Your tracheal stenosis has been getting tighter, and this dilation will stretch it open. You’ve had this before, so you know what to expect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I had it last month. But I’ve been short of breath again. Any risks this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The risks are low. We’ll monitor you closely. Since you have relapsing polychondritis, we always watch for inflammation, but you’ve done well in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. What happens right after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to recovery, then come back here for overnight monitoring. We’ll check your breathing and oxygen levels. No pain expected, but we’ll manage it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on the floor. The procedure went smoothly—balloon dilation of the trachea and left mainstem was successful. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I don’t feel any pain. Is the biopsy going to be checked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the bronchial biopsy and wash are sent to the lab. Preliminary gram stain shows some white blood cells and gram-positive cocci, but culture results are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. With your history, we often see bacteria in the airway. The stain doesn’t confirm infection. We’ll follow up on cultures, but no antibiotics are needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show a high white blood cell count—21.9. But it’s likely from inflammation due to your polychondritis, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I get more tests? I’ve had Pseudomonas before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re already on it. The acid-fast smear was negative, so no sign of mycobacteria this time. We’ll repeat the CBC as an outpatient to watch the count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Oxygen is off, breathing comfortably. We’re clearing you to go home. You’ll take 40 mg prednisone daily for five days to reduce inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then back to my usual dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep taking your famotidine and losartan. Follow up with interventional pulmonology in four weeks for another check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the biopsy results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those will come through follow-up. Call the pulmonology team if you have fever, increased shortness of breath, or bloody secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care, and feel free to call your father to let him know you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Just keep up with your meds and follow-up. Your condition is stable, and we’re managing it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. I’ll make sure to come back for the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll coordinate with rheumatology too, since your polychondritis needs ongoing care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Dr. ___ has been managing that. I’ll keep both visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re all set. Discharge paperwork is ready. Take it easy at home, and we’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for scheduled flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation and bronchial wash due to recurrent tracheal stenosis related to relapsing polychondritis. The procedure was performed without complications, and he remained stable throughout the admission with no respiratory distress or pain. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis, attributed to underlying inflammatory disease rather than infection. He was discharged home with a five-day course of high-dose prednisone, instructions to resume his baseline medications, and follow-up planned with interventional pulmonology in four weeks for review of biopsy and culture results. His breathing improved, and oxygen was successfully weaned prior to discharge.
